doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: The Halo Shampoo jingle and a flood of residual checks
summary: Rogers Brackett asks them to sing a jingle; they delay a trip and find the checks arriving in California.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: And we were there for 11 years, and it was a 15 minute ride to midtown, and a private drive when you got back there. I could leave in the morning, come back at lunch, go back into the City and do whatever you need, and we got into doing television commercials, because at one time we were about ready to go on a trip, to go on the road again, and this friend of ours, the same Rogers Brackett that introduced us to Alec Wilder, called up and said, “listen, I’m doing a jingle tomorrow for Halo Shampoo and we’d like to have you guys sing on it.” And I said, “gee Rogers, we’re leaving tomorrow to take this road trip.”
And our friend Don Payne wrote it too. He had written the jingle.

And let’s see, I said to Rogers I said, “no we can’t do that, we’re leaving tomorrow.” And he said, “well I think it might be worth your while to just postpone leaving one day, it won’t hurt too much.” He said, “it’ll probably mean quite a sum of money.” And I said, “oh really?” He said, “oh yeah.” So okay. We went in, we learned the thing, we recorded it, next day, Jackie and I we sang the thing and it was just like a vocalese.
A very nice thing. It was a bossa nova.
It was just like a simple little, but nice. And it was nothing tricky really.

And we did that, next day we leave, we go, we’re out in San Francisco and we’re starting to get mail. Now here are these big fat envelopes coming in. And I — what is this? Oh yeah, advertising agency. Hey, there’s probably some checks. We opened them up and we looked, nine hundred dollars. Next check, seven hundred, five hundred. Boom, boom, boom, boom. And I said what have we been doing all these years, it’s more money than we’re making for a month working these joints.
You know in jazz you don’t make all that much money, and this is like what, oh, we couldn’t believe it. And for the few minutes that we were in the studio.
